newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel minister to break silence on coalition row.
newsitem.headline: Israel minister to break silence on coalition row.

text.p: Foreign Minister David Levy planned on Monday to break days of silence over a feud with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that threatened Israel's government.
The disgruntled foreign minister cancelled two meetings with Netanyahu in as many days along with an appearance in a parliamentary committee on Monday amid reports he was on the verge of quitting.
"He will hold a press conference at 4 p.m. (1300 GMT) to discuss the situation," said Levy's media adviser Freddy Eytan, declining to elaborate.
Political analysts said Levy was not likely to resign but was also not expected to make remarks that would defuse the coalition crisis.
"He could simply talk very severely about the government's decision making without resigning," said political analyst Shimon Shiffer of the daily Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper.

Levy's rupture with Netanyahu has delayed the appointment of a new finance chief and spawned talk of early elections. Reporters who tried to reach him at his home in northern Israel for scheduled interviews on Monday got a busy signal.
"The foreign minister is not hiding and has nothing to hide...He will say what he has to say when he deems it appropriate," said Eytan.
The 58-year-old Levy, veteran of boundless political intrigue, accuses erstwhile nemesis Netanyahu of operating behind his back in politics and peacemaking.

The latest straw was the disclosure that Netanyahu did not inform Levy of a meeting earlier this month between hawkish cabinet minister Ariel Sharon and top PLO official Mahmoud Abbas, also known as Abu Mazen.
Levy, already complaining that Netanyahu was undermining his position as coordinator of Israel's peace talks with the Palestinians, found out about the meeting from a television report on Friday.

"This government is committing suicide," said Internal Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani. Asked about the likelihood of early elections, he told Israel's army radio: "We're standing at the edge of an abyss. If we jump forward it's clear that's what will happen."
If Levy's five-member Gesher faction bolts the coalition, Netanyahu would be left with a tenuous 61-59 majority in parliament.
Four disenchanted members of Netanyahu's own Likud party failed to support the government in a parliamentary no-confidence vote last week.
With Levy sidelined, ex-general Sharon has taken centre stage, vying for a meeting with the foreign minister to iron out coalition wrinkles after talks on Sunday with Netanyahu.

Sharon, 69, has demanded a seat on Netanyahu's three-member "kitchen cabinet" which directs peacemaking with the PLO. Political sources say Levy and Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai, the other members of the inner forum, are opposed.
Netanyahu has postponed naming Sharon as finance minister until the coalition row is settled.

Palestinians are concerned Sharon, a champion of Jewish settlement expansion in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, will further snarl peacemaking, already deadlocked over the start of work on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem last March.
Both Levy and Mordechai are viewed as relative moderates in Netanyahu's coalition of religious and right-wing parties.

The Moroccan-born Levy, a former construction worker who draws his support mainly from Sephardic Jews of Middle Eastern descent, was the first cabinet member in Netanyahu's government to meet Palestinian President Yasser Arafat last year.
